implementation_notes: The industrial C++ realization treats the envelope as a library type: pack the domain message into google::protobuf::Any (a type-url header plus serialized payload), attach infrastructure metadata as gRPC client metadata (x-format, authorization, correlation-id), and UnpackTo at the destination before the domain layer runs. Any plus the metadata bag replace the hand-written envelope class entirely; the classic POD-header form is only justified when no protobuf/gRPC stack is in the build or the wire format must stay byte-compatible with a legacy peer.
pitfalls: UnpackTo returns false when the Any's type_url does not match the compiled message; ignoring that return value turns a schema mismatch into silently empty domain objects.
gRPC metadata travels in HTTP/2 headers and is size-limited (servers commonly cap request headers around 8 KiB), so it is not a place for large envelope fields.

variants.name: POD header + length-prefixed buffer
variants.idiom_name: hand-rolled struct header + network byte order framing
variants.implementation_notes: Without a protobuf/gRPC stack the envelope is a POD header struct serialized in network byte order (htonl/htons) followed by the payload bytes; std::vector<std::byte> owns the framed buffer and the receiving side validates the decoded length before handing the payload view onward. This is a manual realization - every field addition is a wire-format change - so prefer the protobuf variant unless the peer's format is fixed.
pitfalls: Byte order and packing are entirely yours to get right: without a fixed packing pragma the compiler may pad the header differently from the peer.
The header and payload are two memcpy calls; a mismatch in the length field between them is the classic framing bug.
